concurrent-training.short: Training for strength and for endurance in the same period, either in the same session or on different days.

interference-effect.short: Smaller gains in strength, power or muscle size when endurance training is added to strength training, compared with doing the strength training alone.

hypertrophy.short: Growth of a muscle because its fibres get thicker.

explosive-strength.short: How fast you can produce force, as in a jump or the first push of a sprint, rather than the most force you can reach with all the time you need.

mtor.short: A protein in the cell that works as a main switch for building new muscle protein. Lifting, protein in food and insulin turn it on.

heavy-strength-training.short: Lifting loads of about 80% or more of your one-repetition maximum, so heavy that only a few reps (about 4–10) are possible in a set.

repetition-maximum.short: The heaviest load you can lift a set number of times. A 4 RM load is the most you can lift four times; 1 RM is the one-rep max.

muscle-csa.short: The area of a slice straight across a muscle, measured on a scan. It is a measure of muscle size.

wingate-test.short: A 30 s all-out sprint on a bike against a fixed resistance. It gives peak power (the best second or so) and mean power over the 30 s.

pedro-scale.short: A 10-point checklist of how well a trial was run (random allocation, blinding, follow-up and so on). Higher is better; 4–5 out of 10 means fair to poor.

maintenance-training.short: A reduced dose of training, often one session a week, meant to keep gains already made rather than build new ones.

osteoporosis.short: Bones so thin and weak that they break easily. Osteopenia is the milder stage before it. Both are judged by bone mineral density.
